t: Numbers With Repeated Digits — Counting the Complement
o: We must count integers in [1, n] containing at least one repeated digit. Checking every number up to n = 10^9 is far too slow, so instead we count its complement: numbers with **all distinct** digits, then return n minus that count. In Example 1 (n = 20), only 11 has a repeat, so the answer is 1; in Example 2 (n = 100) the repeats are 11..99 plus 100 itself, giving 10. The constraint n <= 10^9 means n has at most 10 digits, so any per-digit or per-position algorithm runs in constant time.
k: Answer = n − (count of numbers ≤ n whose digits are all distinct); counting distinct-digit numbers is much easier than counting repeated ones directly.
Distinct-digit counts decompose into permutations: a k-digit number uses 9 × 9 × 8 × ... choices because no leading zero and each later digit avoids previously used ones.
For numbers with the same length as n, walk n's digits left to right, placing a smaller unused digit at the first divergence point and freely permuting the remaining positions.

a.i: Simply test every integer from 1 to n by converting it to a string (or extracting digits into a set) and checking whether any digit repeats. This directly mirrors the problem statement and is trivially correct, but with n up to 10^9 it performs up to a billion checks, so it only serves as intuition and a correctness reference on small inputs.
s: For each x from 1 to n, collect the digits of x into a set while scanning.
If at any point a digit is already in the set, increment the counter and move on.
Return the counter after scanning all values.
a.t: O(n · log₁₀ n) — each of the n numbers requires scanning its ~log₁₀ n digits; far too slow for n = 10^9.
a.sp: O(log₁₀ n) — the digit set holds at most one entry per digit of x.

a.n: Approach 2: Combinatorial Counting of Distinct-Digit Numbers (Optimal)
a.i: Count how many positive integers ≤ n have all-distinct digits, then subtract from n. Numbers shorter than n are counted purely combinatorially: a d-digit number has 9 choices for its first digit (no zero) and then 9, 8, ... choices for subsequent digits, giving 9 × P(9, d−1). For numbers with exactly the same digit-length as n, we scan n's digits left to right keeping a set of used digits; at position i we may place any smaller unused digit and then freely arrange the remaining L−i−1 positions from the still-unused digits, contributing P(available, remaining) numbers. If n's own digit was already used we stop early; if we finish the scan without conflict, n itself is distinct-digit and adds 1.
s: Define perm(m, k) = m × (m−1) × ... × (m−k+1), with perm(m, 0) = 1.
Add contributions of all lengths d < L: 9 × perm(9, d−1) for each d from 1 to L−1.
Scan n's digits left to right with a used-digit set; at index i try each digit strictly less than s[i] (starting from 1 at index 0, else 0) that is unused, adding perm(10 − |used| − 1, L − i − 1).
If s[i] is already used, break; otherwise mark it used and continue.
If the loop completes without breaking, add 1 for n itself; return n − total.
a.t: O(L²) where L ≤ 10 is the number of digits of n — the outer scan runs L times and each inner digit loop calls an O(L) permutation product; effectively constant time.
a.sp: O(L) — one boolean array/set of size 10 for used digits plus the digit string.

w: In an interview, mention the brute force briefly to show understanding, then pivot immediately to the complement-counting technique, which is the expected solution. Key pitfalls: forgetting that the first digit cannot be 0 when counting shorter numbers; mishandling the case where n itself has all-distinct digits (the final +1); and off-by-one errors in the available-permutation argument (after fixing a smaller digit at position i, there are 10 − |used| − 1 remaining choices for the next slot). Edge cases worth testing: n = 1 (answer 0), single-digit n (answer always 0), n = 11 (answer 1), and n = 10^9. Likely follow-ups: generalize to counting numbers with all distinct digits in [l, r], or solve it with a classic bitmask digit-DP with tight-bound state — same complexity, more general template.
